## Introduction

### Overview

In Exercises 1--5, you'll continue exploring the RNA-seq results from
[this week's lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd).
In Exercises 6--8, you'll turn your analysis into a polished Quarto report,
render it from a subfolder, and render it for GitHub,
practicing with the Quarto material from
[week 14](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd).
In Exercise 9, you'll use Claude to extend your analysis to all pairwise comparisons,
and to review your report.

::: callout-tip
#### Lecture page exercises
Make sure to do any of the exercises on this week's lecture page that we did
not do in class.
Also, if you struggled with any of the exercises we did do in class,
go over those again.
:::

### Setting up

1. Open Positron and connect to OSC
   [like in week 12](/week12/w12b_r-basics.qmd#setup-starting-positron-and-connecting-to-osc),
   and open your `week15` folder.

2. Install the pheatmap package, which you'll use to make heatmaps,
   by running the following in the R console:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   install.packages("pheatmap")
   ```

3. Create a new Quarto document `week15/w15_exercises.qmd`,
   with a YAML header with a title, your name, the date, and `embed-resources: true`.

4. These exercises build on the DESeq2 object that you saved
   [in the lecture](w15a_rnaseq.qmd#exporting-the-results).
   If you didn't run that code yet, do so in your lecture document first.
   Then, add the following chunk to the top of your exercises document,
   which will load the packages and recreate the objects from the lecture that you'll need:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
library(DESeq2)
library(pheatmap)
library(tidyverse) # Load last (see the lecture)

# Load the DESeq2 object that you saved in the lecture
dds <- readRDS("results/DE/dds.rds")

# Recreate some other objects from the lecture
meta <- as.data.frame(colData(dds))
dds_vst <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds)
res_rc24 <- results(
  dds,
  contrast = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi")
)
res_df <- res_rc24 |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("gene_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(DEG = padj < 0.05)
```

```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE, warning=FALSE}
library(DESeq2)
library(pheatmap)
library(tidyverse)

# TODO: Replace with a regenerated full-data 'assets/week15/dds.rds'.
# This older object has the same counts as the lecture's count table,
# but ERR IDs (ERR10802863 = S63, etc.), so rename the samples:
dds <- readRDS(here::here("assets/week15/dds_full_but-old.rds"))
colnames(dds) <- sub("^ERR108028", "S", colnames(dds))
meta <- as.data.frame(colData(dds))
dds_vst <- varianceStabilizingTransformation(dds)
res_rc24 <- results(
  dds,
  contrast = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi")
)
res_df <- res_rc24 |>
  as.data.frame() |>
  rownames_to_column("gene_id") |>
  filter(!is.na(padj)) |>
  mutate(DEG = padj < 0.05)
```

## Exercise 1: Volcano plots and outliers

In the lecture's volcano plot, one gene stands out with a very high log~2~-fold change.

1. Figure out the identity of this gene by filtering `res_df`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20)
   ```

   (Interestingly, `res_rc24` contains a second gene with a LFC \> 20,
   which is not in `res_df` because its `pvalue` and `padj` are `NA`:

   ```{r}
   as.data.frame(res_rc24) |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20)
   ```

   See the collapsed box "`NA` values in the DESeq2 results table" in the lecture
   for why p-values can be set to `NA`.)

   </details>

2. Label this gene in the volcano plot.
   To do so, add a `geom_text()` layer to the plot from the lecture,
   with its own `data` argument: a data frame with only this gene.
   You'll also need to map the `label` aesthetic to the gene ID column.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   outlier <- res_df |> filter(log2FoldChange > 20)

   res_df |>
     ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) +
     geom_point() +
     geom_hline(yintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = "dashed") +
     # Add the label, in black, and a bit above the point (vjust):
     geom_text(data = outlier, aes(label = gene_id), color = "black", vjust = -1) +
     scale_color_manual(values = c("grey60", "firebrick")) +
     labs(title = "relictum vs. control at 24 hpi") +
     theme_bw()
   ```

   </details>

3. Next, you'll plot the expression levels of individual genes,
   starting with the most highly significant DEG.
   First, get the ID of this gene:

   ```{r}
   top_gene <- res_df |>
     arrange(padj) |>
     head(n = 1)

   top_gene$gene_id
   ```

   DESeq2 has a plotting function, `plotCounts()`, but its plots are not very good.
   We will still use that function, but only to quickly extract the counts
   for our gene of interest in the right format for plotting, using `returnData = TRUE`:

   ```{r}
   focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts(
     dds,
     gene = top_gene$gene_id,
     intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
     returnData = TRUE
   )

   head(focal_gene_counts)
   ```

   Now, you can make the plot:

   ```{r}
   focal_gene_counts |>
     # Treatment along the x-axis, gene counts along the y, color by treatment:
     ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) +
     # Plot separate "facets" with the different time points:
     facet_wrap(vars(time)) +
     # Add a boxplot with a partly transparent (alpha) color:
     geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
     # _And_ add individual points:
     geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
     # Plot styling (e.g., we don't need a legend):
     theme_bw() +
     theme(legend.position = "none")
   ```

4. Make the same plot for the gene with the very high log~2~-fold change.
   How would you interpret this?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   focal_gene_counts <- plotCounts(
     dds,
     gene = "LOC120431476",
     intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
     returnData = TRUE
   )

   focal_gene_counts |>
     ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) +
     geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
     geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
     facet_wrap(vars(time)) +
     theme_bw() +
     theme(legend.position = "none")
   ```

   Wow! It looks like in every single time + treatment combination, all but one (or in one
   case, two) of the samples have zero expression, but there are several extreme outliers.

   For our focal comparison at `24hpi` (left panel/facet), comparing `control` vs `relictum`,
   it looks like the difference between these two groups is solely due to the one outlier
   in `relictum`. Nevertheless, even the multiple-testing corrected p-value (`padj`) is
   significant for this gene:

   ```{r}
   as.data.frame(res_rc24) |>
     rownames_to_column("gene") |>
     filter(gene == "LOC120431476")
   ```

   So, we have to be careful with taking our statistical results at face value, and need to
   visualize important genes!

   </details>

5. Plot one or two more of the most highly significant DEGs.
   Do they have similar expression patterns across treatments and time points
   as the top DEG?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For example, for the second most highly significant DEG:

   ```{r}
   top_genes <- res_df |>
     arrange(padj) |>
     head(n = 3)

   plotCounts(
     dds,
     gene = top_genes$gene_id[2],
     intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
     returnData = TRUE
   ) |>
     ggplot(aes(x = treatment, y = count, fill = treatment)) +
     facet_wrap(vars(time)) +
     geom_boxplot(alpha = 0.5, outlier.shape = NA) +
     geom_point(size = 4, shape = 21, position = position_jitter(w = 0.1, h = 0)) +
     theme_bw() +
     theme(legend.position = "none")
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 2: A customized PCA plot

1. Compare the PCA plot with different numbers of included genes.
   (Hint: figure out how to do so by looking at the help by running `?plotPCA`.)

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   The `ntop` argument sets the number of genes (with the highest variance) to use,
   which is 500 by default:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 100, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"))
   plotPCA(dds_vst, ntop = 5000, intgroup = c("time", "treatment"))
   ```

   </details>

2. Customize the PCA plot: can you "separate" treatment and time point
   (different shapes for one variable, and different colors for the other),
   like in Fig. 1 of the paper?

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for some hints for PCA plot customization_</summary>

   In the plot we made in the lecture, each combination of
   time point and treatment has a distinct color --- it would be better to use **point
   color** only to distinguish one of the variables, and **point shape** to distinguish the
   other variable (as was also done in the paper's Fig. 1).

   To be able to customize the plot properly, we best build it from scratch ourselves, rather
   than using the `plotPCA` function. But then how do we get the input data in the right
   shape?

   A nice trick is that we can use `returnData = TRUE` in the `plotPCA` function, to get
   plot-ready formatted data instead of an actual plot:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   pca_df <- plotPCA(
     dds_vst,
     ntop = 500,
     intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
     returnData = TRUE
   )
   ```

   With that `pca_df` dataframe in hand,
   it will be relatively straightforward to customize the plot using your knowledge
   of ggplot2.

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   First, get the data in the right format, as explained in the hint:

   ```{r}
   pca_df <- plotPCA(
     dds_vst,
     ntop = 500,
     intgroup = c("time", "treatment"),
     returnData = TRUE
   )
   ```

   Second, extract and store the percentage of variance explained by different
   principal components, so you can later add this information to the plot:

   ```{r}
   pct_var <- round(100 * attr(pca_df, "percentVar"), 1)
   pct_var
   ```

   Now we can make the plot:

   ```{r}
   pca_df |>
     ggplot(aes(x = PC1, y = PC2, color = treatment, shape = time)) +
     geom_point(size = 5) +
     labs(
       x = paste0("PC1 (", pct_var[1], "%)"),
       y = paste0("PC2 (", pct_var[2], "%)")
     ) +
     scale_color_brewer(palette = "Dark2", name = "Infection status") +
     scale_shape(name = "Time points") +
     theme_bw() +
     theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 3: More DEGs

1. The paper's Table 1 reports the numbers of **up- and downregulated** DEGs separately.
   Find these numbers for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:**

   ```{r}
   # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame
   as.data.frame(res_rc24) |>
     # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant
     filter(padj < 0.05) |>
     # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE
     dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0)
   ```

   - **Solution using base R:**

   ```{r}
   # Down-regulated (relictum < control):
   sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

   # Up-regulated (relictum > control):
   sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 0 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
   ```

   </details>

2. The paper's Table 1 also reports the number of DEGs with an **absolute LFC \> 1**.
   Find out how many up- and downregulated DEGs with an absolute LFC \> 1
   we have for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` comparison.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   - **Solution using tidyverse/dplyr:**

   ```{r}
   # First we need to convert the results table into a regular data frame
   as.data.frame(res_rc24) |>
     # Then we only select the rows/genes that are significant
     filter(padj < 0.05, abs(log2FoldChange) > 1) |>
     # If we run count() on a logical test, we get the nrs. that are FALSE v. TRUE
     dplyr::count(log2FoldChange > 0)
   ```

   - **Solution using base R:**

   ```{r}
   # Down-regulated (relictum < control):
   sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange < -1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)

   # Up-regulated (relictum > control):
   sum(res_rc24$log2FoldChange > 1 & res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
   ```

   </details>

3. Extract the results for one or more **other contrasts** in the paper's Table 1,
   and compare the numbers of DEGs with those in the table.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   For example, for `cathemerium` vs. `control` at 24 hpi:

   ```{r}
   res_cc24 <- results(
     dds,
     contrast = c("group", "cathemerium_24hpi", "control_24hpi")
   )
   sum(res_cc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 4: Heatmaps

Rather than plotting expression levels for many individual genes,
you can create "heatmap" plots to plot dozens (possibly even hundreds) of genes at once.

1. Make a heatmap of the top-25 most highly significant DEGs
   with the `pheatmap()` function, by running the code below.

   First, create a vector with the IDs of these genes,
   by sorting the results table by adjusted p-value,
   keeping its first 25 rows, and extracting the gene IDs:

   ```{r}
   top25_DE <- res_df |>
     arrange(padj) |>
     head(n = 25) |>
     pull(gene_id)
   ```

   (`pull()` extracts a single column from a data frame as a vector.)

   Unlike some of the functions in the lecture, `pheatmap()` can't directly use the DESeq2 object:
   you have to extract and subset the normalized count matrix,
   and also pass the metadata to the heatmap function:

   ```{r}
   # We need a normalized count matrix, like for the PCA
   # We can simply extract the matrix from the normalized dds object we created for the PCA
   norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst)

   # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest
   # ([rows, columns]: select rows by gene ID, and, by leaving it empty, all columns)
   norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_DE, ]

   # Sort the metadata
   meta_sort <- meta |>
     arrange(treatment, time) |>
     select(treatment, time)
   ```

   Now you can create the plot:

   ```{r}
   pheatmap(
     norm_mat_sel,
     annotation_col = meta_sort, # Add the metadata
     cluster_cols = FALSE, # Don't cluster samples (=columns, cols)
     show_rownames = FALSE, # Don't show gene names
     scale = "row", # Perform z-scaling for each gene
   )
   ```

   Notes on the code and plot above:

   - The z-scaling with `scale =` makes sure you can compare genes with very different
     expression levels: after all, we're interested in relative expression levels across
     samples/sample groups.
   - `pheatmap` will by default perform hierarchical clustering both at the sample (`col`)
     and gene (`row`) level, such that more similar samples and genes will appear closer to
     each other.
     Above, we turned clustering off for samples, to keep them in their by-group order.

2. Make a heatmap with the top-25 **most highly expressed** genes
   (i.e., genes with the highest mean expression levels across all samples).

   <details><summary>{{< fa lightbulb >}} _Click here for a hint: how to get that top-25_</summary>

   ```{r}
   norm_mat <- assay(dds_vst)
   top25_hi <- names(sort(rowMeans(norm_mat), decreasing = TRUE)[1:25])
   ```

   </details>

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   # In the normalized count matrix, select only the genes of interest
   norm_mat_sel <- norm_mat[top25_hi, ]

   # Sort the metadata
   meta_sort <- meta |>
     arrange(treatment, time) |>
     select(treatment, time)

   # Create the heatmap
   pheatmap(
     norm_mat_sel,
     annotation_col = meta_sort,
     cluster_cols = FALSE,
     show_rownames = FALSE,
     scale = "row"
   )
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 5: Adding gene information to the DE results

The gene IDs in the results table, like `LOC120423768`, don't tell you much about the genes.
In week 13, you used the gene annotation table `genes.tsv`,
which has a description and biotype for each gene.
Here, you'll add this information to the DEGs.

1. Read the file `/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv` into a data frame `genes`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   genes <- read_tsv("/fs/ess/PAS3493/share/week13/genes.tsv")
   ```

   ```{r, echo=FALSE, message=FALSE}
   genes <- read_tsv(here::here("assets/week13/genes.tsv"))
   ```

   </details>

2. Convert `res_rc24` to a data frame,
   and move its row names (the gene IDs) into a column called `gene_id`
   (hint: `rownames_to_column()`).

3. Add the gene information to this data frame with `left_join()`,
   and look at the descriptions of the top-10 DEGs.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   res_genes <- res_rc24 |>
     as.data.frame() |>
     rownames_to_column("gene_id") |>
     left_join(genes, by = "gene_id")

   res_genes |>
     arrange(padj) |>
     select(gene_id, description, log2FoldChange, padj) |>
     head(n = 10)
   ```

   The two top DEGs are chymotrypsins,
   including `LOC120423767`, the gene plotted on the
   [optional plotting self-study page](/bonus/r-plotting.qmd#box-plots-of-gene-counts).

   </details>

4. How many of the DEGs (adjusted p-value below 0.05) are protein-coding genes,
   and how many are lncRNAs?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   res_genes |>
     filter(padj < 0.05) |>
     count(biotype)
   ```

   </details>

## Exercise 6: A polished Quarto report

Use the Quarto material from [week 14](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd) to turn
your `w15_exercises.qmd` into a nicely formatted report.

1. Add the following to your YAML header:
   a table of contents, a theme of your choice,
   and `execute` options that hide all warnings and messages in the document.

2. Add a header for each exercise,
   and a sentence or two of Markdown text above or below each plot that describes what it shows.

3. Hide the code (but not the output) of the setup chunk at the top of your document
   with a chunk option.

4. Give your volcano plot from Exercise 1 a figure caption and a custom width and height
   (see the [figure options](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#figure-options) from week 14).

5. In your text, report the number of DEGs for the `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi`
   comparison using **inline code**, so the number is computed when you render the document.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   - The YAML header:

     ```yaml
     ---
     title: "Week 15 exercises"
     author: "Jane Doe"
     date: 2026-11-30
     format:
       html:
         embed-resources: true
         toc: true
         theme: cosmo
     execute:
       warning: false
       message: false
     ---
     ```

   - The setup chunk:

     ````markdown
     ```{{r}}
     #| echo: false
     library(tidyverse)
     # [...]
     ```
     ````

   - The volcano plot chunk:

     ````markdown
     ```{{r}}
     #| fig-cap: "Volcano plot for relictum vs. control at 24 hpi"
     #| fig-width: 8
     #| fig-height: 6.5
     res_df |>
       ggplot(aes(x = log2FoldChange, y = -log10(padj), color = DEG)) +
       # [...]
     ```
     ````

   - Inline code to report the number of DEGs:

     ```markdown
     We found `r "\x60r sum(res_rc24$padj < 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)\x60"` DEGs
     for the relictum vs. control comparison at 24 hpi.
     ```

   </details>

6. Render the document and check that everything looks the way you intended.

## Exercise 7: Rendering from a subfolder

Here, you'll run into the
[working directory issue](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#the-working-directory-when-rendering-and-the-here-package)
from week 14, and fix it with the `here()` function.

1. In the terminal, create a folder `reports` inside your `week15` folder,
   and move your `w15_exercises.qmd` into it.
   Then, render the document.
   Why does this fail?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   With `week15` as your working directory in the terminal:

   ```bash
   mkdir reports
   mv w15_exercises.qmd reports/
   ```

   Rendering fails at the `readRDS()` line, with an error that the file can't be opened.
   The working directory when rendering is now `week15/reports`,
   so the relative path `results/DE/dds.rds` points to `week15/reports/results/DE/dds.rds`,
   which doesn't exist.

   </details>

2. In the terminal, create an empty file `.here` in your `week15` folder,
   so that `here()` will treat `week15` as the top-level folder.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```bash
   touch .here
   ```

   </details>

3. Install and load the _here_ package,
   and change the `readRDS()` line in your setup chunk to use `here()`.
   Then, render the document again,
   and check that the setup chunk also still works when you run it interactively.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Install the package in the Console:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   install.packages("here")
   ```

   Then, in the setup chunk:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   library(here)
   # [...]
   dds <- readRDS(here("results/DE/dds.rds"))
   ```

   `here("results/DE/dds.rds")` now always points to `week15/results/DE/dds.rds`,
   both when rendering (working dir `week15/reports`)
   and when running code interactively (working dir `week15`).

   </details>

## Exercise 8: Output for GitHub

Here, you'll render your report to GitHub-Flavored Markdown
and view it on GitHub, like you can do for your final project
(see the tip on [showing your rendered output on GitHub](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#the-yaml-header-revisited) in week 14).

1. Add `gfm` as a second output format in your YAML header.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```yaml
   format:
     html:
       embed-resources: true
       toc: true
       theme: cosmo
     gfm: default
   ```

   </details>

2. Render the document to both formats in the terminal.
   Which new files and folders were created?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   With `week15` as your working directory in the terminal:

   ```bash
   quarto render reports/w15_exercises.qmd
   ```

   Besides the HTML file, this creates a Markdown file `reports/w15_exercises.md`,
   and a folder `reports/w15_exercises_files` with the plots as PNG files.

   </details>

3. Open the `.md` file in Positron, and look at it with the Markdown preview.
   How are the plots included in the document?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Unlike the self-contained HTML file,
   the `.md` file doesn't contain the plots themselves.
   Instead, it links to the PNG files in the `_files` folder,
   for example:

   ```markdown
   ![](w15_exercises_files/figure-commonmark/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png)
   ```

   That's why you need to commit both the `.md` file and the `_files` folder
   to your GitHub repository.

   </details>

4. Turn your `reports` folder into a Git repository,
   and commit the `.qmd`, `.md`, and `.html` files, and the `_files` folder.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```bash
   cd reports
   git init
   git add w15_exercises.qmd w15_exercises.md w15_exercises.html w15_exercises_files
   git commit -m "Add week 15 exercises report"
   ```

   </details>

5. Create a new repository on GitHub,
   connect your local repository to it, and push,
   like in the [week 6 exercises](/week06/w6_exercises.qmd#exercise-1-github).

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   After creating an empty repository on GitHub
   (without a README or any other files):

   ```bash
   # (replace <SSH-URL-to-repo> with your repo's SSH URL,
   #  which looks like 'git@github.com:<github-username>/<repo-name>.git')
   git remote add origin <SSH-URL-to-repo>
   git push -u origin main
   ```

   </details>

6. On GitHub, click on the `.md` file and then on the `.html` file.
   How do they look?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   GitHub displays the `.md` file as a formatted document, including the plots.
   The `.html` file, on the other hand, is shown as raw HTML code
   (or, because the embedded plots make it a large file,
   GitHub may only offer to show the raw file or download it).

   </details>

## Exercise 9: Going further with Claude

In this exercise, you'll use Claude to take the analysis beyond the lecture,
and to review your report.
Keep working in your `reports/w15_exercises.qmd` document,
with your `week15` folder open in Positron.
Because your `reports` folder is now a Git repository,
you can see exactly what Claude changed with `git diff`,
and undo any changes you don't want.

### Instructions for Claude

1. Create a [`CLAUDE.md` file](/week09/w9a_claude.qmd#persistent-instructions-with-claude.md)
   in your `week15` folder.
   Briefly describe the project,
   and add the R conventions from this course that you want Claude to follow.
   Include at least these:
   use the tidyverse and the `|>` pipe,
   use `here()` for file paths,
   and don't put `install.packages()` in a Quarto document.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see an example_</summary>

   ```{.markdown .file filename="CLAUDE.md"}
   # Week 15: RNA-seq differential expression analysis

   - This folder contains a differential expression analysis with DESeq2
     of mosquito RNA-seq data (_Culex pipiens_ infected with two _Plasmodium_ species),
     in the Quarto document `reports/w15_exercises.qmd`.
   - The DESeq2 object is saved in `results/DE/dds.rds`.

   ## R conventions

   - Use tidyverse functions and the native pipe `|>`.
   - Use `here()` for all file paths, and never use `setwd()`.
   - Don't add `install.packages()` to Quarto documents:
     tell me which packages to install instead, and I'll install them in the console.
   - Load all packages in the first code chunk of a document.
   - Add new code in new code chunks, each under a Markdown header,
     with a sentence that explains what it does.
   ```

   </details>

### All pairwise comparisons

In the lecture, you extracted the results for one of the 6 pairwise comparisons in the paper,
and in Exercise 3, you did so for one or more others.
Here, you'll have Claude do this for all 6 at once.

2. Ask Claude to add a section to your report that extracts the DE results
   for all 6 pairwise comparisons in Table 1 of the paper,
   and makes a table with the numbers of up- and downregulated DEGs for each comparison.
   Review Claude's edit before you accept it, and then run the new code.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see an example_</summary>

   Claude's version will differ each time you ask, but here is one example:

   ```{r}
   contrasts <- list(
     rc24 = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "control_24hpi"),
     cc24 = c("group", "cathemerium_24hpi", "control_24hpi"),
     rcat24 = c("group", "relictum_24hpi", "cathemerium_24hpi"),
     rc10 = c("group", "relictum_10dpi", "control_10dpi"),
     cc10 = c("group", "cathemerium_10dpi", "control_10dpi"),
     rcat10 = c("group", "relictum_10dpi", "cathemerium_10dpi")
   )

   res_all <- map(contrasts, function(contrast) {
     results(dds, contrast = contrast) |>
       as.data.frame() |>
       rownames_to_column("gene_id")
   })

   deg_summary <- res_all |>
     list_rbind(names_to = "comparison") |>
     filter(padj < 0.05) |>
     summarize(
       up = sum(log2FoldChange > 0),
       down = sum(log2FoldChange < 0),
       .by = comparison
     )

   deg_summary
   ```

   The code uses two functions from the tidyverse that we didn't cover:
   `map()` runs a function for each element of a list
   (here, for each comparison),
   and `list_rbind()` combines a list of data frames into a single data frame.

   </details>

3. Check Claude's work:

   - Which 6 comparisons did Claude pick,
     and is the "focal" group listed first in each `contrast` vector?
   - Do the numbers for `relictum_24hpi` vs. `control_24hpi` match the ones you found
     in [Exercise 3](#exercise-3-more-degs)?
   - Did Claude follow the instructions in your `CLAUDE.md`?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   - The paper compares each _Plasmodium_ species (_P. relictum_ and _P. cathemerium_)
     with the controls,
     and the two species with each other,
     at each of the two time points.
     In each `contrast` vector, the first group is the focal group:
     for example, a positive log~2~-fold change for `rc24` means that a gene
     is more highly expressed in `relictum_24hpi` than in `control_24hpi`.
     If Claude switched the two groups in a comparison,
     its numbers of up- and downregulated genes for that comparison are switched as well.
   - The numbers should match exactly.
     If they don't, find out what Claude did differently:
     for example, it may have also filtered by log~2~-fold change,
     or used `pvalue` instead of `padj`.

   </details>

4. Ask Claude to visualize the overlap between the sets of DEGs of the 6 comparisons
   with an "**upset plot**",
   which is the type of plot in Fig. 2 of the paper.
   Install any packages that Claude's code needs in the console.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see an example_</summary>

   Here is an upset plot made with the _UpSetR_ package:

   ```{r, eval=FALSE}
   install.packages("UpSetR") # Run this in the console
   ```

   ```{r}
   #| warning: false
   #| fig-width: 9
   #| fig-height: 5
   library(UpSetR)

   # A list with a vector of DEG IDs for each comparison
   deg_ids <- map(res_all, function(res) {
     res |>
       filter(padj < 0.05) |>
       pull(gene_id)
   })

   upset(fromList(deg_ids), nsets = 6, order.by = "freq")
   ```

   </details>

5. In an upset plot, the bars on the left show the number of DEGs in each comparison,
   and each bar at the top shows the number of DEGs in a combination of comparisons,
   as marked by the connected dots below it.
   Find the bar for the DEGs shared by `rc24` and `cc24` only.
   Then, compute the number of DEGs that these two comparisons have in common yourself,
   with the `intersect()` function,
   which returns the elements that are in both of two vectors.
   Why are these two numbers different?

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   ```{r}
   length(intersect(deg_ids$rc24, deg_ids$cc24))
   ```

   `intersect()` returns all DEGs that are shared by `rc24` and `cc24`,
   which is more than the bar for `rc24` and `cc24` only.
   That's because each gene is counted in just one bar of an upset plot:
   the one for the exact combination of comparisons in which it is a DEG.
   So, the bar for `rc24` and `cc24` only counts genes that are DEGs
   in those two comparisons and _none_ of the others,
   while genes that are also a DEG in, for example, `rcat24`,
   are counted in another bar.
   To get the `intersect()` result from the plot,
   you'd have to add up all bars whose dots include both `rc24` and `cc24`.

   </details>

### A reproducibility review

   Then, ask Claude to review your report for reproducibility,
   and to suggest changes without making them yet.
   Then, let it make only the changes you agree with,
   and check them with `git diff`.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   With `week15/reports` as your working directory in the terminal:

   ```bash
   git add w15_exercises.qmd
   git commit -m "Add all pairwise comparisons and upset plot"
   ```


   </details>

7. Which of Claude's suggestions did you accept, and why?
   Compare them with the guidelines in the
   [week 14 lecture](/week14/w14a_quarto.qmd#structuring-your-quarto-document).

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   </details>

### Learning about your genes

8. In [Exercise 5](#exercise-5-adding-gene-information-to-the-de-results),
   you saw that the two top DEGs at 24 hpi are chymotrypsins.
   Ask Claude what is known about the function of chymotrypsins in mosquitoes,
   and to give you sources for its answer.
   Open one of these sources, and check that it says what Claude says it does.

   <details><summary>{{< fa check-circle >}} &nbsp; _Click to see the solution_</summary>

   Claude will likely tell you that chymotrypsins are proteases
   in the mosquito midgut that help digest the blood meal.

   When checking a source, look for the specific claim that Claude based on it,
   and not just for the right topic.

   </details>
